headlines.article_text: Bank earnings October 2026: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Four of the largest U.S. banks reported third-quarter results on Tuesday: JPMorgan Chase , Wells Fargo , Goldman Sachs and Citigroup . Bank of America and Morgan Stanley will post earnings on Wednesday. The quarter was dominated by headlines around artificial intelligence, IPO uncertainty, high fuel prices and rising borrowing costs. The banks that reported Tuesday put up mixed results. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets and the largest in the world by market capitalization, posted a rare miss. Goldman Sachs, meanwhile, blew past revenue estimates, led by strong equities trading. Earnings calls with company executives at JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs are underway. Here's what you need to know: JPM posts a rare earnings miss WFC is out with mixed results GS reports a massive revenue beat Citi's earnings report caps off the morning JPMorgan's CFO says deals are being 'delayed' Dimon says AI will 'benefit mankind enormously' 2 Min Ago Wells Fargo CEO: Customer base remains strong Scharf said on the call with analysts that the company's customer base is "still strong." "Our underwriting criteria recognize that at some point consumer credit conditions will weaken," Scharf said. "To be clear, we do not see signs of this yet, but we know that cycles are inevitable." – Laya Neelakandan 3 Min Ago Wells Fargo says it's devoting 'significant management time' to AI Charles Scharf, chief executive officer of Wells Fargo & Co., during a Bloomberg Television interview in New York, US, on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images Wells Fargo's Scharf said on the call with analysts that the company is "devoting significant management time and resources" to building out its AI capabilities. Internally, he said the bank is using AI to write code and launch marketing campaigns faster as well as to improve risk management processes. Externally, it's developing AI to improve the customer experience. "We will also evaluate how third-party models and agents can provide value-added capabilities to our clients, while at the same time considering the potential risk these tools can introduce for both our clients and Wells Fargo," Scharf said. – Laya Neelakandan 6 Min Ago Goldman Sachs sees strong demand for AI buildout David Solomon, CEO Goldman Sachs, speaking on CNBC's Squawk Box at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland on Jan. 22nd, 2026. Oscar Molina | CNBC Solomon said Goldman Sachs sees a huge opportunity for financing in the AI buildout, but it's being selective about the risk it underwrites and the capital it commits. "No one knows how the demands for capital and compute will evolve as the broader AI ecosystem matures," he added. But he said more is going to get built and more financing is going to be necessary. "In our conversations with clients, demand for compute significantly, significantly exceeds supply at the moment, creating opportunities to help develop financing structures to meet that capacity shortfall," Solomon said. Still, Solomon cautioned that there might be pressure on rates as the financing needs grow, which would affect returns and the viability of certain projections. He also said the bank recognizes the broader concerns about AI and frontier models that have been acting on their own. "Like other transformative technologies, AI presents significant opportunities, but also significant risks that must be carefully assessed and managed. ... We must enable innovation and also demand responsibility," he said. — Ritika Shah and Michele Luhn 9 Min Ago Wells Fargo's Scharf says headcount decreased Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said on a call with analysts that headcount continued to decline in the third quarter, down 2% from the prior period, 8% year over year and 30% from its peak in the second quarter of 2020. Scharf said the company's headcount has decreased every quarter for the past six years. – Laya Neelakandan 12 Min Ago JPMorgan Chase says it wouldn’t be immune to an AI meltdown In an aerial view, the Stargate Oracle AI data center campus is seen on August 26, 2026 in Abilene, Texas. Brandon Bell | Getty Images JPMorgan Chase won't be immune to a major reversal in the artificial intelligence buildout, the bank's chief financial officer said Tuesday, warning that the entire industry would be impacted in that scenario. The bank is monitoring its exposure to the massive spending on data centers and computing infrastructure by AI companies, CFO Jeremy Barnum said on the earnings call. "Our exposures are still quite modest in the context of our overall wholesale exposure, but that's not the same as saying that we would be immune to a major change in sentiment in the AI space," Barnum said. "I would be surprised if anyone, frankly, was immune to that at this point." The comments underscore the growing stakes for the financial system as hyperscalers race to expand computing capacity and demand enormous amounts of capital. There will be $7.6 trillion in total global AI capital expenditure over the next five years, according to a Goldman Sachs estimate. Barnum said financing is being spread across banks and other parts of the capital markets, adding that the industry must consider whether the broader system can absorb the spending and whether AI investment could crowd out other financing needs. "It's not just traditional construction lending; now increasingly it's working capital revolvers," Barnum said. "You also see it in the equity markets. It's kind of everywhere. And so you really need to be running stress [tests] that test your resilience to a meaningful change in the overall theme." — Hugh Son 15 Min Ago It's a top- and bottom-line beat for Goldman Sachs Goldman Sachs' earnings per share of $17.01 is now comparable to LSEG consensus analysts of $13.02, making for a staggering beat on both the top and bottom lines. — Sara Salinas 23 Min Ago Wells Fargo conference call begins Wells Fargo executives have started a conference call with analysts to discuss the company's third-quarter earnings results. – Laya Neelakandan 30 Min Ago Solomon says deal backlog is 'robust' Andrey Rudakov | Bloomberg | Getty Images Goldman Sachs CEO Solomon said clients are still coming to the bank for significant transactions, citing the $13 billion Hugging Face sale to Nvidia and Integer Holdings' roughly $6 billion sale to KKR as examples. "We entered the quarter with our highest backlog in five years, and even with exceptionally strong revenue production in the quarter, our backlog remains very robust, reflecting the strength and breadth of client engagement across our leading investment banking franchise," he said. — Ritika Shah 36 Min Ago Dimon says JPMorgan won’t allow external AI agents within the bank Jamie Dimon, chief executive officer of JPMorgan Chase & Co., during a Bloomberg Television interview on the sidelines of the JPMorgan Tech Stars Conference 2026 in London, UK, on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. Jose Sarmento Matos | Bloomberg | Getty Images JPMorgan won't allow outside AI agents to operate inside the bank, Dimon said Tuesday, citing risks to the company and its customers as tech firms including Meta and OpenAI release autonomous assistants. "We're not going to allow just any… outside agent to come in inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon told analysts on the company's earnings call. The bank is developing tools to defend against potential misuse of AI agents, which can take actions on behalf of users with limited human intervention, Dimon said. headlines.article_text: Micron, Seagate, Western Digital sink as chip sell-off deepens Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Chip stocks tumbled Tuesday, continuing to fall as the sell-off spilled into Asian and European markets. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress on a new chip structure, intensifying chip competition. Intel and Broadcom CEOs have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom. In this article 9984.T-JP ASML STM IFX-DE SKHY Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images Chip stocks fell on Tuesday, extending a sell-off sparked by worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition. Memory chip giant Micron slipped about 5% while other memory-related names such as SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital also sank. SanDisk fell 5% while Seagate and Western Digital both dropped 6%. The slide, which followed declines on Wall Street on Monday, comes as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT . Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. CXMT is China's leading rival to the likes of Micron and South Korean heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics . Analysts broadly see CXMT as trailing the U.S. and South Korean memory leaders, which means any advancement from the Chinese firm could add more competition to the market leaders. "Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling. "In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email. CXMT shares closed 2.8% lower in Shanghai. Micron, Seagate, SanDisk, Western Digital stock chart. 'Vulnerable' AI sentiment? Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected. But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share. "More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said. He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape. "I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks. watch now VIDEO 4:30 04:30 Tech shakedown spreads as U.S. heavyweights face fresh selling Squawk Box Europe Global tech stocks slump Adding fuel to the sell-off was a post by Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, who said China has the ability to scale production once it figures out how to manufacture something. "When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined," Musk said on Monday. European chip stocks also sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open. Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 7.4% — both hitting their lowest levels since August. SK Hynix's U.S.-listed stock was down around 5% in premarket trading. In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.5%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry through its huge investment in OpenAI, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 7.2%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 2.9%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell over 5%, Disco lost 4.7% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.9%. The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. headlines.summary: The iPhone maker also announced the new Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini.
headlines.article_text: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub to showcase Siri AI Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Apple announced the new HomeView that starts at $299. The iPhone maker also announced the new Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini. HomeView will act as a voice-controlled smart home hub for Apple devices and was built to showcase new Siri AI abilities. In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT John Ternus, chief executive officer of Apple Inc., during a product unveiling event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Apple on Tuesday announced a new home hub called HomeView . Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13. Tuesday's launch event is the second under new CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000. Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price. The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month. Apple said that HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music. Apple's HomeView can be placed on a table or mounted on a wall. Apple "It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's chief marketer Greg Joswiak said in a statement. Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users. Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch. But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus. Apple said on Tuesday that its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales but also helps further lock customers into its own ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone. HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house. Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone. Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories. But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage. It also comes as new boss Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster. Apple's new Apple TV 4K got a price hike from $199 to $299, and comes after a similar price increase earlier this year, after Cook said that memory costs for Apple were unsustainable. headlines.summary: Pharmaceutical sales jumped 7.7% in the quarter ⁠to $16.76 billion, but medical technology division sales rose just 2.5% to $8.6 billion.
headlines.article_text: Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) earnings Q3 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article JNJ Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 8:52 08:52 Johnson & Johnson CFO Joseph Wolk on the company’s Q3 results Squawk Box Johnson & Johnson reported a slightly higher-than-expected profit on Tuesday, driven by strong sales of its immune disease treatment, Tremfya, and said it plans to spin off its hips-and-knees business next year. The company said late last year it intended to spin off its orthopedics unit, DePuy Synthes, into a standalone company, marking its second major spinoff as it sharpens its focus on higher-growth healthcare segments. Chief Financial Officer Joe Wolk said in an interview with CNBC that the company is targeting mid-2027 for the spinoff. "We're not cash strapped. We don't have to pursue a deal that maybe is not optimal," Wolk told CNBC. "We can sit this out for a little bit, separate the business sometime next year." Global alternative asset manager Apollo Global Management is in talks to acquire the orthopedics unit in a ​deal that could value it at close to $20 billion, Bloomberg News reported in September. The company's shares fell 2% before the bell. Middle East conflict weighs on MedTech J&J CFO Wolk told Reuters in an interview that the Middle East conflict, austerity measures in Europe, and pricing in China continued to weigh on international results, "but maybe in a little bit more pronounced way." He said the Middle East conflict, which has driven up fuel costs at home and abroad, has not yet affected the company's costs but has hurt sales in the region. "These are countries that still value and actually want premium healthcare systems, think Kuwait, UAE, Saudi Arabia. They pride themselves on having solid healthcare, very good healthcare," Wolk said. "But their budgets now are being resourced and allocated towards defense." Medical technology division sales rose only 2.5% to $8.6 billion overall, but missed estimates of $8.71 billion, according to LSEG data. Outside the U.S., the division's sales were essentially flat. In MedTech, cardio and surgery drove the miss, J.P. Morgan analyst Chris Schott said. The company raised its full-year reported sales forecast to about $101.2 billion at the midpoint, up from $101.1 billion previously. It increased its adjusted earnings forecast range with a new midpoint of $11.10 per share, up from $11.04. Sales at its Abiomed heart pump business also remained slow after a UK study earlier this year raised questions about using Impella pumps during certain high-risk ​coronary procedures. Quarterly pharmaceutical sales jumped 7.7% to $16.76 billion. Tremfya sales rose 68% to $2.4 billion, beating analysts' estimates of about $2.19 billion, while Stelara sales, which face generic competition, fell 54% to $716 million, still well above Wall Street expectations of $591 million. Tremfya has increasingly replaced lost Stelara revenue following recent approvals in inflammatory bowel diseases. Sales of blood cancer treatment Darzalex rose about 16% to $4.24 billion, short of analyst expectations of $4.4 billion. J&J shares closed at $263.73 on Monday. They have risen 27% this year, outperforming both the broader market and most healthcare peers. The company posted third-quarter revenue of $25.4 billion, above analysts' average estimate of $25.28 billion, and adjusted earnings of $2.59 per share also topped Wall Street expectations of $2.54.
